source.version: Journal version of record: Nature Human Behaviour, Volume 9, June 2025, pp. 1107-1109, Matters Arising (received 9 December 2024, accepted 12 March 2025, published online 14 May 2025), arising from Lee and Chung, Nature Human Behaviour (2024). The PDF has 10 pages: 3 article pages (journal pp. 1107-1109) followed by 7 pages of the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary. The Supplementary Information (including Supplementary Table 1) is not in this PDF.
source.title_on_document: ChatGPT decreases idea diversity in brainstorming

paper_design_summary: A Matters Arising reanalysis of the public data from Lee and Chung (2024), whose experiments randomized participants to complete creative challenges with or without ChatGPT (comparison arms: unaided humans or web search); each participant submitted one idea. The authors compute, for each condition's pool of ideas, the fraction of unique idea concepts (ideas whose pairwise Universal Sentence Encoder cosine similarity exceeds 0.8 count as overlapping) and compare it across conditions in each of Lee and Chung's experiments (1, 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 5). Experiment 2b also includes a ChatGPT-only arm of AI-generated ideas.

arms.name: ChatGPT-assisted
arms.description: Participants instructed to use ChatGPT to generate their idea.

participants.who: Lee and Chung's participants; population not described in this document.
participants.quote: Each participant submitted one idea, which external evaluators rated on multiple creativity dimensions, including innovativeness and usefulness.

ai_tool.how_used: Participants were instructed to use ChatGPT while generating their idea; details not given in this document.

task.description: Creative challenge; the specific task of Experiment 1 is not stated. Lee and Chung's tasks are described generally as gift ideas, designing toys from everyday objects, and repurposing household items.

outcomes.name: Fraction of unique idea concepts in the condition's idea set (threshold 0.8)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Unique fraction = number of unique concepts / total ideas in the set; two ideas overlap when the pairwise cosine similarity of their Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings exceeds 0.8. Robustness (Supplementary Information, not in this PDF): thresholds 0.75 and 0.85; alternative metrics: aggregated comparisons of similarity scores, pairwise comparisons of similarity scores, mean edge distance in minimum spanning trees.

contrasts.reported: Unique fraction: Web-search-assisted 0.96 vs ChatGPT-assisted 0.74 (bar labels; error bars are 95% CIs for individual proportions, not printed numerically). Text: AI-aided sets less diverse in all five experiments, significant in four of five (only Experiment 4 non-significant). Bonferroni-corrected CIs for differences are in Supplementary Table 1 (not in this PDF).
contrasts.locator: p. 1108 (PDF p. 2), Fig. 1 panel 'Experiment 1' and text p. 1108

diversity_detail.metric: Fraction of unique (non-overlapping) idea concepts in a condition's idea set; overlap = cosine similarity > 0.8
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within a condition's idea set (one idea per participant); unique concepts are groups of one or more ideas that do not overlap with any other ideas in the set
diversity_detail.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals for individual proportions (error bars in Fig. 1); Bonferroni-corrected confidence intervals for differences in Supplementary Table 1 (not in this PDF); test not described in the main text
diversity_detail.notes: Higher unique fraction = more diverse, so no sign reversal is needed.

eligibility.reason: Reanalysis of Lee and Chung's (2024) participants, who were randomized to ChatGPT versus no aid or web search (p. 1107). The outcome is a diversity measure computed on the ideas they produced (Universal Sentence Encoder similarity, Fig. 1). Criterion 2 rests on a deduction for Experiment 2a: 96 ChatGPT-aided ideas (p. 1107) and one idea per participant (p. 1107), so at least 96 people in that arm. The document gives no people counts for any arm or experiment, so totals should be taken from Lee and Chung (2024). Per codebook rule 8.4, this reanalysis can supply the across_people primary record for Lee and Chung's sample. The Experiment 2b ChatGPT-only arm is AI-versus-human context only. Design class is set to 'other' because the document does not say whether the experiments were online or in the lab.

one_line_finding: Across Lee and Chung's experiments, ChatGPT-aided idea sets had a lower fraction of unique concepts than comparison sets (e.g., Exp. 1: 0.74 vs 0.96 web search; Exp. 2a: 0.70 vs 0.92 human; Exp. 2b ChatGPT-human 0.41 vs human-only 1.00), significant in four of five experiments (Exp. 4 not significant; p. 1108, Fig. 1).
open_questions: Setting of Lee and Chung's experiments (online panel versus lab) is not stated in this document; design_class is 'other' pending a check of Lee and Chung (2024).
Numbers of participants and ideas per arm are not given except 96 ChatGPT-aided ideas in Experiment 2a; take counts from Lee and Chung (2024) or the OSF data.

Supplementary Table 1 (Bonferroni-corrected CIs for differences, alternative thresholds and metrics, 45 comparisons) is not in this PDF; the online Supplementary Information should be retrieved for contrast-level statistics.

The text counts 'five experiments' with experiment 4 as the only non-significant one, but Fig. 1 shows six panels (2a and 2b separate); which 2a/2b contrast enters the 'five comparisons' is not stated.
Whether the Experiment 2b ChatGPT-only ideas involved any participant is not fully described; the text calls them 'AI-generated ideas'.
Meaning of 'low/high constraints' (Exp. 4) and 'base/high' empathy (Exp. 5) is not described.
Randomization is stated once for Lee and Chung's experiments as a whole, not per experiment.
notes: Matters Arising comment; the PDF has 3 article pages plus 7 pages of the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary (no additional data there). All Fig. 1 values were checked against a high-resolution render of PDF p. 2. The paper reports that with alternative diversity metrics (aggregated similarity comparisons, pairwise similarity comparisons, mean edge distance in minimum spanning trees, and thresholds 0.75 and 0.85) ChatGPT-aided sets were less diverse across experiments, with '37 of the 45 comparisons' statistically significant (p. 1108); these are recorded as robustness variants in measure_detail because their numbers are only in the Supplementary Information. The paper also restates Lee and Chung's finding that ChatGPT raised average rated creativity of individual ideas (p. 1107), but it does not report those numbers, so no with_ai outcome is coded here. Locators use journal page numbers (1107-1109) with PDF page numbers in parentheses.
